<x_0.0869><y_0.0281>_Egypt._<x_0.2129><y_0.0563><class_Caption>

<x_0.2148><y_0.0289>over the continent, they had become a great and powerful people; and from their opposite difpositions and manners, became very frequently enemies to the Egyptians. To one Salatis our author afcribes the deftruction of Thebes in Upper Egypt, fo much celebrated by Homer for its magnificence. But this certainly cannot be the cafe; for Homer wrote long after the time of Jofeph: and we find that even then the Egyptians had the fhepherds in abhorrence, in all probability because they had been grievoufly oppreffed by them. Mr Bruce counts three invalions of thefe people; the first, that of Salatis already mentioned, who overthrew the first dynasty of Egyptian kings from Mesnes, and defroyed Thebes: the second was that of Sabasco or So; for according to him this was not the name of a fingle prince, but of a people, and figni-fics _fhepherds_ and the third, after the building of Memphis, where 240,000 of them were belieged as above mentioned. But accounts of this kind are evidently inconflitent in the highest degree; for how is it possible that the _third_ invasion, antecedent to the building of Jerufalem, could be polterior to the _fecond_, if the latter happened only in the days of Hezekiah?<x_0.9736><y_0.3523><class_Text>

<x_0.2168><y_0.3508>In thefe early ages, however, it would feem that the kingdom of Egypt had been very powerful and its dominion very widely extended; since we find it laid, that the _Batrians_ revolted from Olymandyas, another Egyptian king of very high antiquity, and of whole wealth the moti marvellous accounts are given.<x_0.9746><y_0.4359><class_Text>

<x_0.2158><y_0.4344>After an unknown interval of time from this monarch, reigned Sefotris. He was the first great warrior whose conquetis are recorded with any degree of difficultnefs. In what age of the world he lived, is uncertain. Some chronologers, among whom is Sir Haac Newton, are of opinion, that he is the Seface or Shihak, who took Jerufalem in the reign of Rehoboam the fan of Solomon. Others, however, place him much earlier; and Mr Whifton will have him to be the Pharaoh who refuted to part with the Ifraelites, and was at last drowned in the Red Sea. Mr Bryant endeavours to prove that no fuch perfon ever exilted; but that in his hiflory, as well as that of many ancient heroes, we have an abridgement of that of the Cufhites or Babylonians, who spread themselves over great part of the known world, and every where brought the people in fubjection to them. His reign is reckoned the most extraordinary part of the Egyptian history; and the following feems to be the lealt fabulous account that can be got of it. The father of Sefotris was told in a dream, by the god Vulcan, that his fon, who was then newly born, or perhaps fill unborn, should be lord of the whole earth. His father, upon the credit of this vifion, got together all the males in the land of Egypt that were born on the fame day with Sefotris; appointed nurties and proper perfons to take care of them, and had them treat ed like his own child; being perluaded that they who had been the confiant companions of his youth would prove the molt faithful miniliters and foldiers. As they grew up, they were injured to laborious exercises; and, in particular, were never permitted to take any food till they had performed a courte of 180 furlongs, upwards of 22 of our miles. When the old king imagined they were fufficiently educated in the martial way he deligued them to follow, they were fent by way No 110.<x_0.9912><y_0.9531><class_Text>
